results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book (Digital Compositing for Film and Video, §2.2.2) describes a homemade chroma keyer as a two-stage operation chain you build in your compositor rather than a device. Start by converting the RGB image to HSV, then pipe that into a color curve: the red curve now holds Hue, the green curve holds Saturation, and the blue curve holds Value, so you adjust all three to include or exclude the target object's color ranges [S1].

The step-by-step process:

1. Convert the RGB image to HSV with a color-space conversion operation [S1].
2. Pipe the HSV image into a color-curve operation [S1].
3. Shape the red (Hue), green (Saturation), and blue (Value/Brightness) curves to isolate the desired range, mimicking how a real keyer sets a center color plus H/S/V ranges, sending in-range pixels to white and everything else to black, with tolerances for soft edges [S13].
4. Test on the supplied **Chroma key target.tif** image, a colorful picture made for practicing both chroma and luma keys [S5].

The author's verdict is notably cautious: unlike his homemade luma keyer, where cleverness produces real improvements, a DIY chroma keyer "will probably be more hassle than it's worth" — worth building once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf keyer is hard to improve upon [S2]. This aligns with the broader treatment in the book: commercial keyers such as Keylight and Ultimatte are color difference keyers, and Primatte is a sophisticated 3D chroma keyer [S4][S8].

There's also a fancier variation in §2.2.3: a "3D chroma keyer" built on different principles. Instead of converting to HSV, it bases the key on the specific color of the item of interest, plotting the green backing pixels inside the RGB color cube — a grossly simplified version of Primatte's operating principle [S7]. All required materials are software-side — an HSV conversion and per-channel curves, or the ability to visualize pixels in an RGB cube; the book mentions no special hardware considerations.

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
A nonsquare pixel is one whose width and height aren't equal — a rectangular rather than square picture element — and the book treats this as a property of the video or film format, not something you'd ever see directly. The width-to-height relationship of that single pixel is its **pixel aspect ratio**, which is a completely different number from the aspect ratio of the whole image [S1][S2][S4]. On a properly adjusted computer monitor every pixel is square (1:1) [S1], and HD, graphics software, and computer monitors all use square pixels for creation and display, while old-school SD video uses rectangular ones [S7].

When we state an image's aspect ratio, we usually mean the ratio as it will eventually be viewed. When that displayed ratio differs from the ratio of the stored digital image, the format is said to have **nonsquare pixels** and is often called **squeezed** or **anamorphic** — a term borrowed from the art world, where it described a distorted painting that only looked correct when reflected in a curved mirror [S2][S3]. The book's example formats:

| Format | Pixel geometry |
|---|---|
| Computer monitor (adjusted properly) | Square, PAR 1:1 [S1] |
| NTSC-DV 720×480 / PAL-DV 720×576 | Rectangular (nonsquare) [S7] |
| NTSC analog broadcast | PAR 10:11, pixels slightly taller than wide [S10] |
| Cinemascope film | 2:1 anamorphic squeeze [S6] |

The practical consequence is distortion: a perfectly round circle created in the computer and sent to NTSC without adjustment appears as an ellipse stretched 11/10ths vertically, and whether you must manually compensate depends on your software and hardware [S10]. Cinemascope is used in the book as the "most dramatic" illustration because its two-to-one squeeze shows the issues clearly [S6].

Two working notes matter for compositors. First, systems that "display" nonsquare pixels don't actually stretch what's on your monitor — they apply a temporary geometric unsqueeze to the display only, leaving the underlying image data unmodified [S5]. Second, operations like rotation are dangerous on squeezed images: rotating an anamorphic element directly produces visible distortion, and the correct order is to unsqueeze, rotate, then resqueeze. Even a small 5° rotation leaves a subtle wrongness, so the book's advice is to double-check everything when working with nonsquare pixels [S8].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The "Miscellaneous Drawing Tips" sections come from Francis Glebas's *Directing the Story*, a book about visual storytelling for film, and they treat drawing as story communication: every sketch should be bold, clear, and built around one central idea [S3][S6][S7]. Related passages from the same book add that a drawing should remain readable even if blackened in, with decoration kept inside strong outlines [S1], and that pitches should be drawn with a grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil so they read from across the room [S2].

**Clarity and storytelling**
- Draw for clarity — one idea per sketch; have something to say in your image, don't doodle [S3][S7].
- Highlight the important idea and subordinate everything else to it [S6].
- Don't get too clever — tricky camera angles can make a drawing ambiguous [S6].
- Don't be afraid to redraw and search for the best solution; cut out and rework any part that doesn't work [S3].
- Make outlines interesting, and keep decoration within the main outline so drawings don't get busy [S1].

**Technique and dynamics**
- Draw bold and expressive, and number your drawings [S2][S6].
- Avoid symmetry — it looks cut out; use angles for dynamic asymmetry, and play straight lines against curves for interest [S3][S6].
- Use straight-line symbols for stretches and bent-line symbols for squashes [S6].
- Darken pupils when drawing eyes, and watch body landmarks where bones reach the surface, like hipbones and ribs [S3][S6].
- Draw borders so you have to compose to them [S6].
- Feel the pose: show how the character feels, express what the person is "doing," and feel the emotion kinetically in your own body as you draw [S6].

In the cinema context, these tips all serve one goal — instant legibility for an audience. A storyboard or pitch frame should communicate its single idea at a glance, which is why the book stresses bold linework, clear silhouettes, and subordinating every detail to the main idea [S1][S2][S7].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The book frames the choice as a matter of how dissimilar the two displays are. **Transcoding** applies when the displays differ only in their primary chromaticities: if their black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma are identical, the encoded colors can be converted by linearizing the first display's encoded RGB values, converting them to CIE XYZ, converting those XYZ values to the corresponding RGB values for the second display, and reimposing the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. **Color rerendering** is the recommended solution when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar — first, any color rendering implicitly or explicitly done for the first display is undone, then the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values are color rendered for the second display [S1].

| | Transcoding [S2] | Color rerendering [S1] |
|---|---|---|
| **When used** | Displays match except in primary chromaticities | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions grossly differ |
| **What it does** | Linearize RGB → CIE XYZ → new display's RGB → re-encode | Undo first display's color rendering, then re-render XYZ for the new display |
| **Nature** | Colorimetric conversion between encodings | Appearance transform for a changed viewing environment |

The distinction matters in cinema because color rendering is understood as the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment [S4]. Raw camera encodings leave color rendering to be done downstream, since it is far easier for the visual effects team to render than to undo if a manufacturer has baked it into a non-raw format [S6]. This is exactly the logic behind the ACES workflow: the RRT provides a color-appearance rendering for dark-surround theatrical viewing, with tone compression and saturation controls [S3][S5], and ODTs then modify the RRT data to look correct on each display device [S9]. So when a finished image moves between environments that differ in viewing conditions — a dark theater versus a bright monitor, say — the book's argument is that a simple transcoding of numbers is not enough; the image must be color rerendered for the new display [S1][S2][S4].

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The book's thesis is that affect, fatigue, and injury are **control states** — internal conditions that must change what a character does next, not adjectives attached after the choreography is chosen [S2]. The retrieved material never defines "control state" abstractly; the only definitional statement is functional: these states "must change later action selection and execution," and treating them as post-hoc labels is the error the chapter is built against [S2]. Each of the three gets its own state object, and together they form the input layer to a character's next behavior.

```
affect_update → new valence/arousal/dominance + behavioral effects ─┐
fatigue       → global exertion + local limb capacity               ├─► next action
injury        → capacity limits + compensations                     ─┘   selection
                                                              and execution quality
```

**Affect** is modeled as an appraisal update. On a trigger, appraisal dimensions — goal congruence, controllability, certainty — move valence/arousal/dominance from a prior to a posterior, and that posterior carries concrete behavioral effects: attention narrows, recovery becomes urgent but less mechanically clean, and risk tolerance rises for one recovery attempt [S2]. The cinematic worked example shows the expressive payoff: in a concealed-fear close-up, experienced affect slides from mildly to strongly negative valence, arousal spikes at the final word, and dominance drops then partially recovers, while displayed affect stays near neutral-positive with only moderate arousal and higher dominance [S1][S9]. The underlying valence/arousal structure matches the circumplex literature, where arousal tracks sympathetic nervous system activation and the 2-D structure replicates across psychometric studies [S8][S12].

**Fatigue** is two-layered — global exertion (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) plus local capacity per limb — with coordination effects such as increased step-width variability, longer stabilization after hard redirection, and greater trunk contribution when the right shoulder is taxed [S4]. Mechanically, the handbook proposes a compiler-state accumulator: f(t+Δt) = clamp(f + work + impact − recovery, 0, 1), where f is fatigue, not remaining capacity [S6]. The book is explicit that the work, impact, and recovery terms "must be calibrated; they are not inferred reliably from prose alone" — so what the material does not supply is exactly that calibration, the values that would make the equation runnable [S6].

**Injury** is framed as mechanical consequence plus compensation. The injury object carries region, structural status, pain (0–10) and severity (0–4), effects on load acceptance, flexion tolerance, and push-off capacity, and compensations such as favoring the right leg, shortening left stance, and increasing trunk lean during emergency recovery [S3]. It is marked as uncertain by design — "dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement," confidence 0.70 [S3]. Pain also reaches the voice, affecting breath and its connection to pitch, rhythm, quality, resonance, and intensity, with central-body injuries tending toward lower pitch and peripheral ones toward higher pitch; adrenaline can mask the sensation, so a character may not immediately realize the extent of an injury [S11].

| State | What it encodes | What it changes | Uncertainty flagged |
|---|---|---|---|
| Affect | VAD prior→posterior from appraisal (goal congruence, controllability, certainty) [S2] | Attention, recovery urgency, risk tolerance for one attempt [S2] | No deterministic emotion→movement mapping [S15] |
| Fatigue | Global exertion + per-limb capacity [S4] | Step-width variability, stabilization, trunk compensation [S4] | Update terms must be calibrated, not inferred from prose [S6] |
| Injury | Region, pain/severity, mechanical effects [S3] | Load acceptance, flexion tolerance, push-off capacity + compensations [S3] | "Dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement," confidence 0.70 [S3] |

The three states interact through the same controller rather than living in separate layers: affect shifts attention and one-shot risk tolerance, fatigue degrades the coordination of the very recovery maneuver affect is urging, and injury caps the capacity that maneuver draws on while imposing compensation patterns [S2][S4]. The chapter's main warning applies to all three: research supports kinematic cues to emotion at the population level, not deterministic rules like "anger = always faster" or "fear = always retreat" — character, culture, task, injury, and tactical intent remain moderators [S15]. For the cinema practitioner, the takeaway is twofold: these states are runtime inputs to an embodied control loop, and the concealed-fear example demonstrates the core design opportunity — the experienced state can spike, lag, or deliberately diverge from what the audience sees on screen [S1][S9].

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
Motion in cinema is only readable against a background: in the screen world, visual movement is produced only when an object moves in relation to the frame line, and its motion is gauged by changing position relative to stationary objects in the scene [S8][S3]. The book organizes this into three related patterns.

**Relative movement** is the standard case — the object's position changes against a fixed background object, and the viewer reads the change as motion [S3]. **Induced movement** is the reverse reading: a moving object transfers its movement to a nearby stationary one, so the background appears to move while the true mover looks still [S1]. **Apparent movement** covers the camera-driven version: when the camera pans to follow a car driving a circle around it, the trees in the background sweep by in the opposite direction of the pan, and the viewer transfers that background motion to the car, which reads as moving even though it stays locked in the frame. Block notes that in this case there is still no true relative movement between the car and the frame — the background does the work [S13].

This rests on the definition of object movement: anything that moves in relation to the frame line is a moving object, and every moving object generates a track — the path it traces — which can be actual or virtual [S5]. Continuity of that track from shot to shot is what makes movement flow across cuts, so a new shot's movement ideally picks up where the previous track ended [S7].

Cinematic technique exploits the background for motion in several ways. Tracking alongside a character or vehicle gives greater emphasis to the moving background and the sweep of the motion [S14]. Moving players or the camera between foreground objects, rather than in front of them, introduces motion parallax — the variation in image travel of objects at different distances from the lens — which conveys their position and distance to the viewer [S10]. Pairing a telephoto lens with a circular tracking move around a static subject makes the background appear to revolve rapidly behind the person, an effect used to visualize a character's psychological breakdown [S9].

The counterpoint is that the greatest contrast to object movement is no movement at all: tableau staging, where object motion is minimized in favor of the stationary arrangement of objects in the frame [S2]. Even stillness is legible only because the frame and background hold still — the background is always the reference against which motion, or its absence, is read.

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
Across the editing and sound-design texts in the corpus, sound editing is treated as the postproduction discipline of building the soundtrack layer by layer — and it's considered at least as critical as the picture edit, because an unconvincing or ill-judged soundtrack will undermine visuals no matter how well they're cut [S1][S11].

## What sound editing is

Sound editing is where all sound details are worked out: anything production didn't capture is created in postproduction, and because of the number of tracks involved the sound edit demands many more decisions than the picture edit [S1]. The sound designer is responsible for the overall acoustic experience for the audience, overseeing the many individual tracks — dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley — much as the director of photography shapes the image [S6]. The result is the film's **sound design**: an aural universe of layered dialogue, effects, music, ambient atmospheres, and sometimes voice-overs [S7]. This work is so valued that major awards go to people who do it well [S5].

## Purpose: clarity and believability

The first task is determining the narrative point of the scene and surrounding it with sound that supports it [S1]. The two primary goals of the edit are **narrative clarity and believability** — and believability is the most urgent, because sound is processed by viewers faster than visuals; if it doesn't seem believable, the visuals are undermined and audience involvement is lost [S11]. Creatively, sound manipulates audiences on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels, which is why even "silent" films were always accompanied by music — only technological limits kept them mute [S5]. At the mix level, sound can also separate or link shots and scenes, and imply either the passage of time or continuity of time [S13].

## How the soundtrack gets built

During the rough cut, only the tracks needed for dramatic decisions are edited — dialogue plus occasional scratch music. After picture lock, the editor and sound designer build the multi-track design **one track at a time**, typically 6–16 tracks for a simple film, then equalize and mix everything down to a master, from stereo up to 5.1 surround for cinema [S7]. The mixing phase is where the separation or linking of sounds is decided, often by fading one effect out while fading another up, or by letting one continuing sound bridge two disparate visuals [S13]. During sound editing itself, the editor experiments with manipulating speed and pitch [S2], and the sound editor's overall design serves as the guide for rerecording, transmitted to the director [S3].

Track counts scale dramatically with the production:

| Production type | Tracks |
|---|---|
| Simplest music video | ~2 [S4] |
| Simple film | 6–16 [S7] |
| Feature film | up to ~60 [S13] |
| Blockbuster | 62+ [S4] |
| Cinema delivery format (Sony SDDS) | 8 channels [S2] |

In an integrated tool like DaVinci Resolve's Fairlight page, the mix lives inside the editing application, so picture, effects, color, and sound can all be refined up to mastering — including editing sound effects and narration, recording voiceover, and cleaning up background hum [S10]. Postproduction also gathers or creates sounds that augment and sometimes replace production audio, often generating a new, even more realistic "reality" for the narrative [S9]. Historically, this wasn't always possible: early sound recording and editing were so constrained by synchronization problems that the arrival of sound actually inhibited editing until rerecording and multiple-camera techniques developed [S14].

One detail the corpus doesn't supply: the texts state that sound effects fall into four main categories, but the retrieved passages don't enumerate them — the track types named elsewhere are dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley, but that list isn't explicitly identified as the four categories [S6][S8].

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The book — *Hey Whipple, Squeeze This* — returns to one rule for radio again and again: **write sparely**. Cut the script to the bone and leave room for silence, because silence in radio does the same work that white space does in print: it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S12].

**The rule and why it works**

A :60 spot is a house, a :30 is a tent — less room to begin with. And because most radio spots are promotional, clients will bolt promotional tags onto the end and eat whatever time remains, so you have to start lean [S1]. Spare writing gives the voice talent room to read slowly, quietly, one word at a time, which is exactly where the spot’s power lives [S2]. Even when the concept demands fast, wordy action, stay lean anyway: showing up at the studio with a fat script means editing under pressure and without client approval [S4].

The payoff is near-paradoxical: bare-bones executions “leap out of the radio” precisely because there is so little competing for the listener’s attention [S12]. The book’s working method is practical — cover the wall with concepts, scribbling only the general idea on Post-it notes before any full script is written [S3], and take the grunt work (like writing dozens of “live” radio scripts for a hotel chain) to build the skill, since few copywriters can actually write radio and those who can are treated like gold [S5][S8]. Sparseness also fits the medium’s physics: radio’s canvas is visual and unlimited — a spot can send an entire armored division crashing through a mall to buy burgers — so the words don’t have to carry everything; one impossible image lets the listener’s imagination do the rest [S11].

**What spare sounds like**

The retrieved chapters don’t include a full example script of a spare radio spot. The closest specimens are the armored-division line above — a single short declarative carrying a huge image [S11] — and Lewis Carroll’s sentence quoted as the model: “Sometimes I’ve believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast” [S11]. The supporting craft sources show the same instinct from the opposite direction: overwritten, repetitive lines (“Wow, thanks so much for the gift. I really appreciate the present…”) are exactly what spare writing avoids [S6], and the short-sentence rhythm of surprise — “Men don’t walk on the moon. It’s a long way up. The air is thin.” — is the pattern spare radio aims at [S13]. General dialogue craft agrees: dialogue is music with rhythm and tone, and one-track, explanatory writing is a mark of mediocrity [S7]. Modern voice work formalizes the same move — contractions, fragments, discourse markers, one concrete detail instead of adjective stacks [S9].
